newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico sorghum 97 output rosy, but still importing.
newsitem.headline: Mexico sorghum 97 output rosy, but still importing.

text.p: Mexico's sorghum output for 1997 is seen rising to around eight million tonnes from two million tonnes, the president of the National Association of Sorghum Growers told Reuters.
In an interview, Urbano Ortiz Carranza said that despite the rosy crop outlook for this year the country would still need to import sorghum to make up for the country's traditional deficit.

"The deficit that will need to be complemented will be around 4 million tonnes," Ortiz said, adding that the increased production outlook was based on favorable non-irrigated planting estimates and more surface area under cultivation because of higher prices.
"Good international prices have stimulated the planting of sorghum ahead of other fodder crops," Ortiz, himself a sorghum farmer in the western state of Jalisco, said.
Non-irrigated plantings in Tamaulipas state are about to be harvested from the autumn-winter plantings. Ortiz estimated the state could produce around 2 million tonnes - in line with other outlooks.
Mexican offices of the United Soybean Board (USB) and the American Soybean Association (ASA) said in a joint outlook this week that the Tamaulipas crop will be a record this year.

"Harvest will begin in mid-May and is expected to reach volumes above 2 million tonnes, with a possibility of reaching 2.5 million tonnes if there is good weather throughout the harvest season," the USB/ASA said.
Ortiz said numbers of sorghum farmers have reached around 125,000 this year because of the favorable price outlook. Normally, around 100,000 to 110,000 farmers plant sorghum.
He added around 2.5 million hectares planted with sorghum this year, 30 percent irrigated and 70 percent non-irrigated.
Nonetheless, Ortiz said he expected imports to enter Mexico, especially in the interim harvest period of September and October.
But he warned that sorghum associations around the country were on the alert for poor-quality cheap imports that could upset national pricings.

Sorghum growers criticized the government severely last year for allowing around 250,000 tonnes of sorghum in the country from Argentina, which locals alleged was of poor quality and which rocked national prices.
Ortiz said the association and the Mexican Sorghum Council had been working with poultry farmers and feed manufacturers to foster purchase accords allied with coordinated local plantings.
"The idea is that both farmers and consumers win because both have cut out concerns of finding a buyer or a seller and both see the price of transportation cut to a bare limit," Ortiz added.

On the recent discovery of the ergot fungus in a few, isolated number of Mexican sorghum fields, Ortiz said he believed authorities were taking the sensible approach against the disease by quarantining areas for a length of time to check it and investigate any spreading.

Ergot has been found in Mante, Altamira and San Fernando in Tamaulipas state, Ebano in San Luis Potosi state, San Jose del Valle in Nayarit state and Panuco in Veracruz state, according to Gustavo Frias Trevino, director of the National Phytosanitary Reference.
